In particular, we demonstrate how the hydrodynamic behavior of the field theory is encoded in the low-momentum limit of correlation functions computed using a real-time AdS/CFT prescription, which we formulate. We further establish that field-theory hydrodynamic excitations map onto the lowest quasinormal modes of the AdS black \(p\)-brane geometry. This text reviews recent applications of the anti-de Sitter/conformal field theory (AdS/CFT) correspondence to finite-temperature field theory. Particular attention is given to the way hydrodynamic behavior emerges in the long-wavelength, low-momentum limit of field-theory correlation functions calculated using the real-time AdS/CFT prescription.

Within the gravitational description, hydrodynamic modes in the thermal field theory are identified with the low-lying quasinormal modes of an AdS black \(p\)-brane geometry. This correspondence provides a direct connection between dissipative processes in the field theory and perturbations of the dual black-brane background.

The text also establishes the universality of the shear-viscosity-to-entropy-density ratio for a broad class of strongly coupled theories that admit classical gravity duals. Building on this result, it discusses the conjecture that this ratio has a universal lower bound. Such a viscosity bound may have implications beyond idealized holographic models, potentially offering insight into the behavior of strongly interacting real-world systems, including the quark–gluon plasma and ultracold quantum fluids.

The review develops the real-time AdS/CFT prescription for calculating finite-temperature correlation functions in strongly coupled quantum field theories. In the gravitational description, thermal equilibrium is represented by an asymptotically anti-de Sitter black p-brane, while perturbations of the field theory’s conserved currents and stress tensor correspond to fluctuations of bulk gauge and gravitational fields. Retarded Green’s functions are obtained by solving the linearized bulk equations with incoming-wave boundary conditions at the black-brane horizon and fixed boundary values at the AdS boundary.

In the long-wavelength, low-frequency regime, these correlation functions are governed by hydrodynamics. Their characteristic poles—associated with shear diffusion, charge diffusion, and sound propagation—are shown to coincide with the lowest quasinormal frequencies of the corresponding black-brane perturbations. Hydrodynamic relaxation in the boundary theory can therefore be interpreted geometrically as the decay of low-lying quasinormal modes in the dual spacetime. This correspondence provides a systematic way to extract transport coefficients such as diffusion constants, sound attenuation rates, and shear viscosity from classical gravitational calculations.

A central result is the universality of the shear-viscosity-to-entropy-density ratio for a broad class of strongly coupled theories with two-derivative Einstein gravity duals. Using both Kubo formulas and the absorption properties of black-brane horizons, the review finds

\[
\frac{\eta}{s}=\frac{\hbar}{4\pi k_{\mathrm B}},
\]

or \(\eta/s=1/(4\pi)\) in natural units. The universality of this value follows from the near-horizon dynamics of the transverse graviton and is largely independent of the microscopic details of the boundary theory.

Motivated by this result, the review proposes that \(\hbar/(4\pi k_{\mathrm B})\) may represent a lower bound on the viscosity-to-entropy ratio of physical fluids. Such a bound would distinguish strongly interacting, nearly perfect liquids from weakly coupled gases and could have implications for experimentally accessible systems, including the quark–gluon plasma and ultracold atomic gases. Although later developments show that the bound can depend on the assumptions imposed on the gravitational theory, the relation remains a foundational result in holographic hydrodynamics and an important benchmark for understanding transport in strongly coupled matter.
outputs.L5:
### AdS/CFT: A Possible Bridge Between Gravity and Quantum Physics

The AdS/CFT correspondence is a possible framework for unifying gravity with quantum mechanics. It proposes that a gravitational theory in an anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetime can be equivalent to a conformal field theory (CFT) defined on its lower-dimensional boundary.

This idea is a powerful example of holography: information contained in a volume of space may be fully described by a theory living on its surface. Calculations that are difficult in the gravitational AdS theory can sometimes become more manageable in the corresponding CFT, and vice versa.

Although the correspondence is best understood in highly symmetric theoretical models, it has influenced research on black holes, quantum information, particle physics, and strongly coupled matter. It may also offer clues about how spacetime itself could emerge from quantum entanglement.

AdS/CFT is not yet a complete description of our universe, which does not appear to have AdS geometry on cosmological scales. Nevertheless, it remains a possible path toward understanding quantum gravity and the deeper relationship between geometry, matter, and information.

counterfactuals.output: We review finite-temperature gauge/gravity duality, focusing on the emergence of relativistic hydrodynamics from black-brane dynamics in asymptotically anti-de Sitter spacetimes. We describe the holographic prescription for real-time retarded correlation functions and show how their analytic structure is governed by quasinormal modes of the dual gravitational background. In the long-wavelength, low-frequency regime, hydrodynamic quasinormal modes reproduce diffusion, sound propagation, and constitutive relations of the boundary plasma, while nonhydrodynamic modes determine relaxation and the limits of hydrodynamic behavior. Particular attention is given to transport coefficients extracted through Kubo formulas, especially the shear viscosity-to-entropy density ratio, \(\eta/s\). We discuss the universal result \(\eta/s=1/4\pi\) in two-derivative Einstein gravity, its microscopic interpretation, and its modification by higher-derivative corrections, finite coupling, anisotropy, and broken translational symmetry. We also summarize developments in holographic thermalization, hydrodynamic attractors, and nonequilibrium dynamics. Together, these results establish finite-temperature AdS/CFT as a powerful framework for connecting black-hole perturbation theory with the collective behavior of strongly coupled quantum matter.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize recent applications of gauge/gravity duality to thermal field theory, including the universal viscosity bound and possible relevance to real physical systems.
counterfactuals.output:
Gauge/gravity duality—especially AdS/CFT—maps certain strongly coupled quantum field theories at finite temperature to classical black-hole or black-brane geometries. Thermal observables that are difficult to calculate directly can then be obtained from horizon dynamics and gravitational perturbations.

### Main applications to thermal field theory

- **Transport coefficients:** Retarded correlation functions are computed by studying fluctuations falling into a black-hole horizon. This yields shear and bulk viscosities, conductivities, diffusion constants, and relaxation times.
- **Hydrodynamics:** Long-wavelength black-brane perturbations correspond to hydrodynamic modes in the field theory. Fluid/gravity duality has generated nonlinear relativistic hydrodynamics, including higher-order gradient corrections and estimates of the regime where hydrodynamics remains useful.
- **Thermalization far from equilibrium:** Numerical gravitational collapse and colliding gravitational shock waves model rapid energy deposition and equilibration. These studies show that hydrodynamic behavior can emerge before the pressure becomes isotropic, a phenomenon often called *hydrodynamization*.
- **Spectral functions and probes:** Holography has been used to study current and stress-tensor spectral densities, photon and dilepton production, heavy-quark drag, momentum broadening, quarkonium screening, and jet-energy-loss proxies.
- **Phase structure:** Black-hole transitions model confinement/deconfinement, chiral transitions, superconducting phases, and quantum critical matter. Bottom-up “improved holographic QCD” models are tuned to lattice thermodynamics and used to extrapolate into regimes where direct calculations are difficult.
- **Finite density and strong magnetic fields:** Charged and anisotropic black branes provide models of dense matter, strange metals, magnetized plasmas, and anomalous transport such as the chiral magnetic and vortical effects.
- **Quantum information:** Entanglement entropy, complexity, and information spreading provide additional diagnostics of thermalization. Black-hole calculations imply rapid scrambling and, in many holographic systems, saturation of the chaos bound  
  \[
  \lambda_L\leq \frac{2\pi k_BT}{\hbar}.
  \]

### The viscosity result

For a broad class of isotropic, translationally invariant theories with a two-derivative Einstein-gravity dual,
\[
\frac{\eta}{s}=\frac{\hbar}{4\pi k_B},
\]
or \(1/4\pi\) in natural units. The result follows from the universality of low-frequency graviton absorption at a regular horizon. Kovtun, Son, and Starinets conjectured that
\[
\frac{\eta}{s}\geq \frac{\hbar}{4\pi k_B}
\]
for all fluids.

This is now better regarded as a **benchmark rather than a universal bound**. Higher-derivative gravitational terms—dual to finite-coupling or finite-\(N\) corrections—as well as anisotropy, translation breaking, and other effects can produce smaller values. Consistency requirements such as causality and positivity still constrain how large such violations can be in controlled models.

### Possible relevance to real systems

The most prominent application is the quark–gluon plasma created at RHIC and the LHC. Heavy-ion data are well described by viscous hydrodynamics with a small \(\eta/s\), often inferred to be of order a few times \(1/4\pi\). Holographic shock-wave simulations also reproduce qualitative features such as rapid hydrodynamization, strong collective flow, and efficient energy loss. Holographic models constrained by lattice QCD can give useful semi-quantitative guidance for transport and finite-density behavior.

Other potential connections include ultracold unitary Fermi gases, which also behave as nearly perfect fluids, and strongly correlated electronic materials, where holographic models capture scaling, incoherent transport, and “Planckian” relaxation times of order \(\hbar/k_BT\).

The caveat is that standard holographic theories usually have large numbers of degrees of freedom, strong coupling, approximate conformal symmetry, and often supersymmetric origins. Real QCD and condensed-matter systems lack many of these properties. Thus gauge/gravity duality is most reliable as a source of controlled strong-coupling examples, universal mechanisms, and qualitative benchmarks—not as a first-principles numerical solution of real-world thermal matter.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output: In gauge/gravity duality, hydrodynamic excitations of a finite-temperature field theory are encoded in the lowest quasinormal modes of an asymptotically anti-de Sitter black \(p\)-brane. Linearized bulk perturbations, classified into shear, sound, and charge-diffusion channels, obey ingoing boundary conditions at the horizon and normalizable conditions at the AdS boundary. Their discrete complex frequencies coincide with poles of the dual retarded correlation functions. In the long-wavelength limit, modes whose frequencies vanish as momentum \(k\to0\) reproduce hydrodynamic dispersion relations, such as \(\omega=-iDk^{2}+\cdots\) for diffusion and \(\omega=\pm c_s k-i\Gamma_s k^{2}+\cdots\) for sound. The corresponding coefficients determine transport data, including diffusion constants, viscosities, and sound attenuation. Higher quasinormal modes remain gapped and describe nonhydrodynamic relaxation. Thus, the low-lying black-brane spectrum provides a gravitational realization of emergent hydrodynamics and its approach to local equilibrium.

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a research-paper overview of real-time AdS/CFT methods for computing low-momentum thermal correlators and proving the universality of the shear viscosity-to-entropy density ratio.
counterfactuals.output:
# Real-time AdS/CFT, thermal correlators, and the shear-viscosity ratio

## Abstract

Real-time gauge/gravity duality computes finite-temperature response functions by solving classical bulk fluctuation equations in an asymptotically anti-de Sitter black-brane geometry. The essential retarded prescription is to impose ingoing boundary conditions at the future horizon and differentiate the renormalized on-shell action with respect to boundary sources. At low frequency and momentum, these correlators exhibit hydrodynamic poles and determine transport coefficients through Kubo formulas. For any isotropic translationally invariant plasma whose bulk dual is governed by two-derivative Einstein gravity with a regular horizon, the transverse graviton controlling shear response behaves as a minimally coupled massless scalar. Its radially conserved low-frequency flux relates the boundary shear viscosity to the horizon area, yielding
\[
\frac{\eta}{s}=\frac{1}{4\pi}
\qquad (\hbar=k_B=1).
\]
This result is universal within the Einstein-gravity regime, but not in general: higher-derivative interactions, finite-coupling effects, anisotropy, translation breaking, or nonminimal graviton couplings can modify it.

---

## 1. Thermal states from AdS black branes

A homogeneous thermal state of a \(d\)-dimensional quantum field theory is represented holographically by an asymptotically AdS\(_{d+1}\) black brane. A convenient metric is
\[
ds^2=g_{tt}(r)\,dt^2+g_{rr}(r)\,dr^2+g_{ij}(r)\,dx^i dx^j,
\]
with a regular future horizon at \(r=r_h\) and Hawking temperature
\[
T=\frac{1}{4\pi}
\left.
\sqrt{\frac{-g_{tt}'(r)}{g_{rr}^{(-1)\prime}(r)}}
\right|_{r_h},
\]
with the precise form depending on the radial parametrization. The entropy density is given by the Bekenstein–Hawking area law,
\[
s=\frac{A_h}{4G_{d+1}V_{d-1}}.
\]

Boundary operators are sourced by asymptotic values of bulk fields. For example,
\[
\delta S_{\rm QFT}
=\frac12\int d^dx\,h_{\mu\nu}^{(0)}T^{\mu\nu},
\]
so a bulk metric perturbation \(h_{\mu\nu}(r,x)\) sources the stress tensor.

The classical gravity approximation requires large effective \(N\) and strong coupling, so that bulk loops and stringy higher-derivative terms are suppressed.

---

## 2. Why Euclidean continuation is insufficient by itself

Euclidean AdS/CFT computes Matsubara correlators from smooth fields on the Euclidean black-hole “cigar.” In principle, retarded functions follow by analytic continuation,
\[
i\omega_n\rightarrow \omega+i0^+,
\]
but this can obscure:

- causal boundary conditions;
- dissipation and horizon absorption;
- hydrodynamic poles;
- general Schwinger–Keldysh correlators;
- nonequilibrium or time-dependent states.

Real-time holography directly implements causal response. The horizon is crucial: infalling disturbances are absorbed, providing the gravitational representation of thermal dissipation.

---

## 3. Retarded Green functions: the Son–Starinets prescription

Consider a bulk field \(\phi\), Fourier decomposed as
\[
\phi(r,x)=\int\frac{d^dk}{(2\pi)^d}
e^{-i\omega t+i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{x}}
\phi(r,k).
\]
For a quadratic action, the on-shell bulk action reduces to a radial boundary term,
\[
S_{\rm os}
=\frac12\int\frac{d^dk}{(2\pi)^d}
\,\phi(-k,r)\,\Pi(k,r)\Big|_{\rm boundary},
\]
where
\[
\Pi(k,r)=\frac{\delta S}{\delta(\partial_r\phi(-k,r))}
\]
is the radial canonical momentum.

Write
\[
\phi(r,k)=\phi^{(0)}(k)F(r,k),
\qquad F(r\to\infty,k)=1.
\]
The retarded prescription is:

1. Solve the linearized bulk equation.
2. Normalize the non-normalizable boundary mode to the source.
3. Impose an **ingoing** condition at the future horizon.
4. Evaluate and renormalize the canonical momentum at the AdS boundary.
5. Differentiate with respect to the source.

Schematically,
\[
G_R(k)
=-\lim_{r\to\infty}
\frac{\Pi(k,r)}{\phi(k,r)}
+G_{\rm ct}(k),
\]
up to source-normalization conventions. Local counterterms affect contact and analytic terms but not dissipative spectral weight or hydrodynamic poles.

Near a nonextremal horizon, the two local solutions behave as
\[
\phi\sim (r-r_h)^{\mp i\omega/(4\pi T)}.
\]
For the Fourier convention \(e^{-i\omega t}\), the minus sign is infalling:
\[
\phi_{\rm in}\sim (r-r_h)^{-i\omega/(4\pi T)}.
\]
This condition makes \(G_R\) analytic in the upper half of the complex \(\omega\)-plane and realizes causality.

The spectral function is
\[
\rho(\omega,\mathbf{k})=-2\,\operatorname{Im}G_R(\omega,\mathbf{k}),
\]
modulo sign conventions. Horizon absorption therefore determines the dissipative part of the response.

---

## 4. Full Schwinger–Keldysh formulation

Retarded correlators can be obtained by the infalling prescription alone, but a complete real-time thermal theory requires a doubled Schwinger–Keldysh contour. Boundary sources \(\phi_1^{(0)}\) and \(\phi_2^{(0)}\) live on the forward and backward time branches. The corresponding bulk construction glues Lorentzian black-hole regions, often with an Euclidean segment preparing the thermal density matrix.

In the \(r/a\) basis,
\[
\phi_r=\frac12(\phi_1+\phi_2),
\qquad
\phi_a=\phi_1-\phi_2,
\]
the quadratic generating functional contains retarded, advanced, and symmetric kernels. Thermal horizon regularity gives the Kubo–Martin–Schwinger relation and the fluctuation–dissipation theorem,
\[
G_{\rm sym}(\omega,\mathbf{k})
=-\coth\!\left(\frac{\beta\omega}{2}\right)
\operatorname{Im}G_R(\omega,\mathbf{k}),
\]
with convention-dependent overall factors.

Thus the same horizon physics that produces absorption also supplies the thermal noise accompanying dissipation.

---

## 5. Low-momentum expansion and hydrodynamic correlators

Hydrodynamics governs the regime
\[
|\omega|,\ |\mathbf{k}|\ll T.
\]
The gravitational calculation implements this as a simultaneous small-\(\omega\), small-\(k\) expansion of gauge-invariant perturbations.

For momentum chosen along \(z\), fluctuations split under the residual transverse rotation group into:

- **tensor/shear-stress channel**, such as \(h_{xy}\);
- **vector/shear-diffusion channel**, involving \(h_{tx}\) and \(h_{zx}\);
- **scalar/sound channel**, involving energy and longitudinal pressure fluctuations.

Gauge-invariant master fields eliminate radial-diffeomorphism redundancy. Their quasinormal modes—ingoing at the horizon and source-free at the boundary—are poles of retarded correlators.

### Shear diffusion

Conservation of transverse momentum gives
\[
\omega=-iD_\eta k^2+\mathcal O(k^4),
\qquad
D_\eta=\frac{\eta}{\epsilon+p}.
\]
For a neutral relativistic thermal state,
\[
\epsilon+p=sT,
\]
so
\[
D_\eta=\frac{\eta}{sT}.
\]
Einstein holography therefore predicts
\[
D_\eta=\frac{1}{4\pi T}.
\]

### Sound

The longitudinal channel contains
\[
\omega_\pm(k)=\pm c_s k-i\Gamma_s k^2+\cdots,
\]
where
\[
\Gamma_s=
\frac{1}{2(\epsilon+p)}
\left[
\frac{2(d-2)}{d-1}\eta+\zeta
\right]
\]
for a neutral fluid in \(d\) spacetime dimensions. Conformal invariance gives
\[
\zeta=0,\qquad c_s^2=\frac{1}{d-1}.
\]

Higher orders in the bulk gradient expansion determine relaxation times and other second-order transport coefficients.

---

## 6. Kubo formula for shear viscosity

Perturb the boundary metric by \(h_{xy}^{(0)}(t)\). Linear response gives
\[
\delta\langle T^{xy}\rangle
=-G_R^{xy,xy}(\omega,\mathbf{0})\,h_{xy}^{(0)}
\]
up to the convention used for metric sources. Hydrodynamics implies
\[
G_R^{xy,xy}(\omega,\mathbf{0})
=P-i\eta\omega+\mathcal O(\omega^2),
\]
possibly plus contact terms. Hence
\[
\eta
=-\lim_{\omega\to0}
\frac{1}{\omega}
\operatorname{Im}G_R^{xy,xy}(\omega,\mathbf{0}).
\]

At zero spatial momentum, the off-diagonal metric fluctuation
\[
\phi(r,t)\equiv h_x{}^y(r,t)
\]
decouples from other fields in an isotropic background. For two-derivative Einstein gravity its quadratic action is that of a minimally coupled massless scalar,
\[
S^{(2)}
=-\frac{1}{32\pi G_{d+1}}
\int d^{d+1}x\,\sqrt{-g}\,
g^{MN}\partial_M\phi\,\partial_N\phi,
\]
up to equivalent normalization conventions.

Its canonical radial momentum is
\[
\Pi(r,\omega)
=-\frac{\sqrt{-g}}{16\pi G_{d+1}}
g^{rr}\partial_r\phi.
\]
The retarded function follows from \(-\Pi/\phi\) at the boundary.

---

## 7. Horizon proof of \(\eta/s=1/(4\pi)\)

### 7.1 Radial conservation at low frequency

The fluctuation equation can be written
\[
\partial_r\Pi(r,\omega)
+\frac{\sqrt{-g}}{16\pi G_{d+1}}
g^{tt}\omega^2\phi(r,\omega)=0.
\]
Therefore, in the \(\omega\to0\) limit,
\[
\partial_r\Pi=\mathcal O(\omega^2).
\]
The response ratio
\[
\chi(r,\omega)=\frac{\Pi(r,\omega)}{i\omega\phi(r,\omega)}
\]
is radially constant to the order relevant for viscosity. It may consequently be evaluated at the horizon instead of the boundary.

This is the membrane-paradigm or radial-RG form of the argument.

### 7.2 Ingoing horizon condition

Ingoing regularity in Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates gives
\[
\partial_r\phi
\simeq
-i\omega\sqrt{\frac{g_{rr}}{-g_{tt}}}\,\phi
\]
near the horizon. Substitution into \(\Pi\) yields
\[
\frac{\Pi}{i\omega\phi}\Big|_{r_h}
=
\frac{1}{16\pi G_{d+1}}
\left.
\frac{\sqrt{-g}}
{\sqrt{-g_{tt}g_{rr}}}
\right|_{r_h}.
\]
For an isotropic black brane, the final factor is the spatial horizon-area density,
\[
\left.
\frac{\sqrt{-g}}
{\sqrt{-g_{tt}g_{rr}}}
\right|_{r_h}
=\frac{A_h}{V_{d-1}}.
\]
Thus
\[
\eta=\frac{A_h}{16\pi G_{d+1}V_{d-1}}.
\]
Using
\[
s=\frac{A_h}{4G_{d+1}V_{d-1}},
\]
one obtains
\[
\boxed{\frac{\eta}{s}=\frac{1}{4\pi}}.
\]

The proof uses only the zero-frequency radial conservation law, horizon regularity, the universal Einstein kinetic term for \(h_x{}^y\), and the area law for entropy. It does not require solving the fluctuation equation throughout the geometry.

---

## 8. Equivalent absorption argument

The same result can be phrased in terms of graviton absorption. The imaginary part of the retarded stress-tensor correlator is proportional to the absorption probability of a transverse graviton by the black brane. For a minimally coupled scalar at zero frequency, the absorption cross section equals the horizon area:
\[
\sigma_{\rm abs}(0)=A_h.
\]
The Kubo formula then identifies
\[
\eta=\frac{\sigma_{\rm abs}(0)}{16\pi G_{d+1}V_{d-1}},
\]
which again gives \(\eta/s=1/(4\pi)\).

The absorption and membrane-paradigm derivations are two formulations of the same conserved radial flux.

---

## 9. Scope of the universality claim

The result is universal for a broad but restricted class of theories:

1. The bulk action is two-derivative Einstein gravity, possibly coupled to matter.
2. The equilibrium geometry has a regular nonextremal horizon.
3. The state is homogeneous and isotropic in the shear plane.
4. The relevant transverse graviton decouples and has the Einstein kinetic normalization.
5. Translation invariance and the standard hydrodynamic interpretation are intact.
6. The classical bulk approximation is valid.

Matter fields may have nontrivial radial profiles without changing the result, provided they do not alter or mix the shear graviton’s effective kinetic term.

The statement is therefore not a theorem about all quantum field theories, nor is \(1/(4\pi)\) an absolute lower bound.

---

## 10. Corrections and violations

### Higher-derivative gravity

Finite-coupling corrections in the boundary theory generate bulk terms such as
\[
R^2,\qquad R_{MN}R^{MN},\qquad R_{MNRS}R^{MNRS},
\]
or string-theoretic \(R^4\) interactions. These modify both:

- the effective horizon coupling of the transverse graviton;
- the entropy, which must be computed using the Wald formula rather than the area law.

Consequently,
\[
\frac{\eta}{s}
=\frac{1}{4\pi}\left(1+\delta_{\rm hd}+\cdots\right).
\]

For five-dimensional Gauss–Bonnet gravity, for example,
\[
\frac{\eta}{s}
=\frac{1-4\lambda_{\rm GB}}{4\pi}.
\]
Positive \(\lambda_{\rm GB}\) can lower the ratio below \(1/(4\pi)\), although causality, positive-energy, unitarity, and UV-completion constraints restrict the allowed coupling.

For large-\(\lambda\) \(\mathcal N=4\) supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory, the leading stringy correction raises the ratio above its infinite-coupling value:
\[
\frac{\eta}{s}
=\frac{1}{4\pi}
\left[
1+\frac{135}{8}\zeta(3)\lambda^{-3/2}
+\cdots
\right]
\]
in a standard convention for the ’t Hooft coupling.

### Other departures

Universality can also fail or require reinterpretation when there is:

- spatial anisotropy, yielding several shear viscosities;
- explicit or spontaneous translation breaking;
- nonminimal mixing between metric and matter perturbations;
- finite-density backgrounds with channel mixing;
- nonrelativistic scaling;
- extremal or singular horizons;
- bulk quantum corrections of order \(1/N\).

In momentum-relaxing systems, the coefficient extracted from \(G_R^{xy,xy}\) remains well defined, but it need not govern a conserved-momentum diffusion pole in the usual way.

---

## 11. Practical workflow for low-momentum correlators

A standard holographic calculation proceeds as follows:

1. **Specify the black-brane solution** and compute \(T\), \(s\), and equilibrium one-point functions.
2. **Classify perturbations by symmetry channel.**
3. **Construct gauge-invariant master variables**, especially in coupled vector and scalar sectors.
4. **Fourier transform** with \(e^{-i\omega t+i k z}\).
5. **Impose infalling horizon conditions**, preferably using regular ingoing coordinates.
6. **Solve perturbatively in \(\omega/T\) and \(k/T\)** or numerically for arbitrary momentum.
7. **Expand near the AdS boundary** into source and response coefficients.
8. **Add Gibbons–Hawking and holographic counterterms** to obtain a finite variational problem.
9. **Differentiate the renormalized action** to obtain the retarded correlator matrix.
10. **Extract poles and low-frequency coefficients**, matching them to hydrodynamic constitutive relations and Kubo formulas.

Constraint equations must be retained: they encode boundary Ward identities such as stress-tensor conservation. Contact terms may depend on renormalization scheme, whereas pole positions and dissipative coefficients do not.

---

## 12. Conceptual interpretation

The universality argument connects three descriptions of the same infrared physics:

- **Boundary hydrodynamics:** viscosity governs stress relaxation.
- **Bulk causal propagation:** the retarded response is selected by infalling horizon conditions.
- **Horizon membrane dynamics:** the low-frequency shear response is fixed by a local horizon coupling.

The radial direction acts as an energy-scale coordinate. At strictly low frequency, the shear transport coefficient does not run between the horizon and the boundary. This converts a boundary many-body transport problem into a horizon calculation.

The value \(1/(4\pi)\) is therefore best understood not as a universal property of all fluids, but as a universal fixed value for strongly coupled plasmas admitting a classical, isotropic, two-derivative Einstein-gravity dual.

---

## Foundational references

counterfactuals.prompt: In one paragraph, describe progress in using AdS/CFT for finite-temperature field theories, covering hydrodynamic behavior, black-brane quasinormal modes, the η/s universality result, and the viscosity-bound conjecture.
counterfactuals.output: AdS/CFT has provided a powerful framework for studying strongly coupled finite-temperature field theories by mapping thermal states to black branes in higher-dimensional gravity. Long-wavelength perturbations of these geometries reproduce relativistic hydrodynamics, while black-brane quasinormal modes correspond to poles of retarded thermal correlators: the lowest modes yield diffusive and sound behavior, and higher modes describe nonhydrodynamic relaxation toward equilibrium. A major result is the near-universal shear-viscosity ratio \(\eta/s=1/(4\pi)\) for a broad class of large-\(N\), strongly coupled theories with two-derivative Einstein-gravity duals. This inspired the Kovtun–Son–Starinets conjecture that \(\eta/s\ge 1/(4\pi)\) in all physical fluids, although higher-derivative gravity, finite-coupling corrections, and some anisotropic or nonrelativistic systems can violate the original bound, so it is now regarded as a benchmark rather than a strict universal law.
